utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We'll be sitting this week pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away on official business of the Tribunal. I was told that Mr. Tieger, you have something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's a scheduling matter, very brief. Pursuant to the Court's suggestion on Friday, we have been attempting to readjust the witness schedule. In the course of that effort, there is a matter that arises that I wanted to alert the Court to as early as possible, because I think some action at this point could remedy that situation. In the week of the 21st of June there will be a witness commencing who must leave on the 24th. If the Court could add one extra hour per day that week on the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd, that would allow the witness to complete his testimony within the time allocated or requested as matters currently stand by the cross-examination schedule. Now, obviously that could be done with the normal four hours one day, six hours another day, five hours another day, but basically that would remedy the difficulty of the witness' schedule for that week. So if I could ask whether it was possible for the Court to check into that possibility and alert us as quickly as possible. That would be of enormous assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will look into the matter. Then we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the only thing I'd add, Your Honours, the witness is coming from very far away, so going back and forth is not a genuine possibility. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness who is supposed to come on 21st June?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate you're coming back to conclude your testimony. Now, you'll bear in mind that your declaration will still apply today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you're ready, we'll start. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everybody. Thank you, Mr. Lynden, for coming back. May I ask you whether we are richer, and have you brought one of your diaries with you? Have we been enriched with an extra diary?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told the Court when I was last here, the diaries -- or my notebooks, rather, I don't have diaries, my notebooks are not in my possession. All our property is currently held in storage, and I -- that's held in the Netherlands, and I have not been in the Netherlands, and, no, I have not been into the storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, Mr. van Lynden, that the media have a decisive influence on public opinion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. In certain cases they can. In other cases, they don't. There is no simple answer to that question. We could write books about that kind of thing, Mr. Karadzic, and I think people have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that your reports, especially your reports, as coming from a respected journalist and respected newspaper or news agency, have a very important role in public opinion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I answered before, possibly some of the reports had an impact. I think a lot of the reports actually didn't have an impact. It's very difficult for -- for me to judge the precise impact that any single report that I sent while I was in a war zone, I can't judge how it is viewed in the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, may we have two photographs put up on our screens, please -- or, rather, on the overhead projector so that we can have a look at them. I'm not going to tender them into evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the ELMO has been activated. Can you proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This caricature that we see here, does that affect the formation of public opinion, for instance?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this before. I don't know where it was published, so I can't really react to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's not very nice for the Serbs and Croats to see this. The one with the U on his cap is a Croat; right? It's not very pleasant.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine this depicts, but as I said, this is the first time I've ever seen it, a Croat on the left, a Serb in the middle, and a Muslim on the right, and I would not imagine that would be pleasant, but as I said before, I don't know who made this, where it was published, who would have seen it. It's a caricature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, obviously a German creation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe it's the first time I've seen or heard of it -- seen it or heard of it as well, Your Honour. I was wondering if this has a 65 ter number or if it was listed as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it has been informed -- you didn't inform the Prosecution that you're going to use this document during your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just received it, Your Excellency, so I just wanted to share it with Mr. van Lynden and show him what impact the media can have on public opinion, but I'm not going to tender it into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not you tender it, we have a rule you have to abide by. You have to inform the Prosecution in advance of the documents you're going to use. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I show another caricature then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder what point it would have, but let's proceed. Whether Mr. van Lynden can make any comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only comment, Your Honour, that I can make is Mr. Karadzic just said, "And show him what impact media can have on public opinion." I'm not sure that this character had any impact on public opinion. I'm not sure where it was ever published. Mr. Karadzic says it's German. What that proves is beyond me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to your next topic. No, it's done. Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, the film that you showed us with the night bombing, you said that it was taken by a Sky News reporter, right, that he filmed it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the film in the reports at the beginning of June were indeed filmed by a Sky News cameraman whom I was with continually while he was filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how was the footage edited?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a picture editor. Also from Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How much -- or, rather, how long was the raw material, the raw filming?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would vary from day to day, but as I recall during those days, certainly minimally two tapes of 30 minutes a day, probably more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the editor would condense it to fit into just a few minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Television news reports -- a news bulletin is usually less than half an hour long. Therefore, most broadcasts would be -- a report would be about a minute to a minute and a half long. In this case, these reports were longer, very long, by the standards of a news bulletin, usually about two and a half to three minutes, but, yes, of course it has to be edited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at least an hour of film was reduced to two or three minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your viewers, the viewers who saw the footage, were they able to gain an impression as to who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, because we told them that most of the -- what they were seeing was incoming into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, you know, that Sarajevo had Serbs and Serb districts and neighbourhoods; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said "most."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the convent, and do you agree that that was a Catholic church convent and throughout it was on Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I don't see the point in connection to the footage that we shot as far as the shelling of Sarajevo was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't on that footage, and the footage wasn't clear either. You couldn't actually see that it was the Catholic church and the convent, which is located on Serb territory right up at the front line or almost up at the front line. What I want to say is that this wasn't stressed sufficiently, that it was a Catholic church on Serb territory, safeguarded very well throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're really wrong here, Mr. Karadzic. Firstly, you are dealing with two completely separate matters, the stories that I did at the beginning of June and a story that I did in September when I was working out of Pale. And we made quite clear in that report that we were in the territory of Sarajevo that was controlled by your forces and that these nuns were there, close to the front lines, and giving food to elderly people living there still. So the two are not connected. The reports at the beginning of June and the report in September are two separate reports at different times, and we did make clear that that convent was within the territory held by your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but although they could have been Serb, too, but what I wanted to say was this was an example where the monastery was not a Serbian one and not Orthodox, yet it was located on Serb territory and nothing happened to it. It was very safe. And I'm not talking about just one of your reports but your reporting in general. But anyway, thank you. Now, do you remember, Mr. van Lynden, one of your reports about the relocation of weapons, and you were shown a very big guy, and you said that his nickname was Zver or "Beast."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know what you're referring to. This is after a deal had been done with the UN agreeing to the withdrawal of your heavy weaponry either completely or to UN collection points and simultaneously the collection of heavy weaponry within Sarajevo to UN collection points. We were taken the day after General Rose had announced that all the heavy weaponry had either been removed or was now under the care of the UN by representatives of your government on a trek north of Sarajevo, and one of the places we stopped, we stopped at several, we saw -- as I remember with this bit, I -- I may be wrong, but I think what he had were heavy mortars, 120-millimetre mortars. I can't remember him being called the Beast, but that may well be -- may have been his nickname. What he showed me was that all the -- he was there, and the heavy weaponry was there, had not been withdrawn, but there was nobody from the UN there, and I remember him quite clearly saying that he'd heard what General Rose had told the world the previous night, that all the heavy weaponry had been withdrawn or was under UN control, and he then said to me, Well, as you can see, that's not the case. He was very willing for the UN to come, but the point was that the UN hadn't come and that was really also the point to the report that we made that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that that young man was referred to as Zver or Beast in that footage. Now, do you remember that his nickname was Medo or teddy bear and that probably your translator -- your interpreter translated it as beast? Do you know the difference between beast or bear or teddy bear?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information, and I don't precisely recall this incident, but people did have nicknames, as far as I can recall, he spoke about this. He was a jovial figure who welcomed us. There was no problem. We were offered a drink. It was very early in the morning, but -- and I had with me, firstly, Jaksa Scekic from Belgrade, who was the producer at that time with me working in Pale; and secondly, we had had someone who -- from your administration who also spoke English. They translated it to me. I didn't make that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask the interpreters to put me right if I'm wrong in what I'm going to say, but Medo, teddy bear, cannot be translated as "beast" but as "teddy bear." The teddy bear is a nice animal, but he was represented as a Serb beast in your report, whereas he was a good natured teddy bear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Excellency, this good natured teddy bear was portrayed as a Serb beast. That's what this is about. In his words in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have the opportunity to bring up the matter later on in your submission. This is the time for you to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Now, may we have called up on e-court, please, document 1D1211 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. van Lynden, let me ask you this: Do you remember that on the 8th of April, 1993, a military patrol at Ilidza, near the airport, in a convoy organised by a respected humanitarian organisation, found weapon -- found ammunition hidden in the humanitarian aid convoy?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall right now, I was not in Bosnia on the 8th of April, 1993, and, no, I do not remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But are you -- do you only limit your knowledge about the events in Bosnia to the period when you were there, or did your television station send out reports about everything?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had correspondence almost permanently in Bosnia, other correspondence, but you cannot expect me to recall every single incident that happened in Bosnia, and certainly not in the periods when I was there. And even when I was there, I would be focusing on one particular area and not on everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see this document? It's a text from the "The Independent," an article from the "The Independent," dated the 22nd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you have to say to that, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that certain people, also within the UN, I believe that this is the case. I've never seen -- was never shown convincing evidence that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And all the things that you reported about the Serbs, did you have convincing evidence of that and reports from the Presidency and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we reported we believed to be the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you should believe the United Nations and their doubts and their beliefs as to who was doing the shooting, the shooting at civilians.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the UN is a large organisation. There are also differences of opinion within the United Nations. We did check with the United Nations, as I've testified earlier within this trial, about precisely about what was happening, about the front lines, about the breaking of -- of cease-fires, about the levels of -- of shelling on one district or another. Were they always entirely correct? Probably they weren't. We did our best. I have never -- I have asked when I was in Sarajevo, specifically also when General Rose was there, because although General Rose wasn't saying it publicly, as far as I was aware then, there were indications that he felt that some of the fire was indeed directed, as this report would say, but we asked for a report and we never got one. Without conclusive evidence being shown to me, I was not going to make a report of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D240.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D01226 called up next, please. Thank you. That's the first page. May we turn to page 2, please. And I hope we have a translation. Yes, we seem to. Yes. Yes. Page 2 in both the Serbian and English please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a bulletin from the military security of the Muslim army, and in the highlighted portion it says that: "The military security service has knowledge of the fact that the citizens of Sarajevo are leaving the city also with the help of fake press accreditation. "Actually, journalists who have already been accredited in Sarajevo have received accreditations from their networks for individuals who are supposedly engaged by news teams and are thereby allowing them to leave the city," and in brackets it says "probably in return for monetary gain." Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never handed out our accreditations ourselves to anybody. Locally, we brought people in only. We certainly never ever took anybody out of Sarajevo. We did not transport other people. We were there, sent by news organisation in Britain, and we didn't deal with that kind of thing. What we did do was take a lot of mail out, for instance, from Sarajevo, and we were once stopped at one of your check-points and we were told that we were not allowed to -- to do that kind of thing, that it was an illegal activity, until they saw that many of the letters were actually addressed to people in Serbia, and then we were allowed to continue with that mail. But as far as smuggling people out on false accreditations, certainly not. We absolutely did not deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you think, Mr. van Lynden, about the regime or any regime in any city that one cannot get out of unless one has some documents, permits, whatever?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the nature of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you report to your company that you could not leave the city of Sarajevo if you do not have a foreign accreditation, or, rather, the citizens of Sarajevo cannot travel, cannot leave town unless they have some accreditation? Were you aware of that? You were aware of that, weren't you? You knew that people could not leave town. Did you report about that? Did you say that there was an inside blockade within Sarajevo and that they were not allowing people to leave town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly reported that the people of Sarajevo could not get out. We also reported -- I mean, they couldn't get out normally as we could as accredited foreign media with UN accreditation, although often that was difficult for us as well. We also reported that people did try to get out. For instance, a lot of people from Sarajevo tried or sometimes managed, sometimes not, to cross the airport and get out from Sarajevo into Budimir, and although I never saw it, I believe that a tunnel was later dug to facilitate people coming in and out of the town that was besieged by your forces. Where -- I mean, you've asked me a whole number of questions. One of them is that you're saying that these people were not allowed out because their people didn't let them out. That would be true up to a point, but the basic point about Sarajevo is that it was besieged by your forces who would have shot these people or taken them prisoner if they had tried to get out. They couldn't walk out or drive out like we did. That was an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the Serb side fired at people who were crossing over to the Serb side? Give us one single example of that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where were you? That's what happened in the war. People couldn't leave Sarajevo. They would have been fired upon. In fact, even buses which were organised to get small children out of Sarajevo were fired upon. Now, can I say categorically that that was only done by your forces? No, I can't. Was I in the bus? No, I wasn't. But the basic truth of the siege of Sarajevo was that the people were besieged in that town, and that even if they had got their side to say, yes, you may leave, there had to then -- usually, the only people who could then take them out would be the UN. That did happen on occasion, but not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, who would they show this permit to when they wanted to cross over to Serb territory? Would they show it to the Serb authorities or their own authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you cross a front line like we had to, you would have to first show your papers on one side and then drive through the no man's land that always existed and then show it on the other side. So you would have to show it to both. There were organised procedures at certain occasions when people were allowed to leave. We indeed filmed an old woman crossing from Grbavica across the Miljacka into Bosnian territory when we were with your forces in September, and we showed that. That had been an organised -- between the two sides that this old lady should be allowed to cross. I don't know the particulars of that old lady because we were not told about it, but we were able to film her and we put her in that report. So there were organised instances of people crossing from one side to the other, but for the normal population to just say, "Well, I'm now leaving town because I don't like it here anymore because I'm being shot at, and I'd like to go to another part of the country," that was impossible for them. They would have known that they risked certainly arrest, probably imprisonment, and possibly death on arriving on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They risked arrests and death from the Serb side you mean? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From either side. If someone had just tried to walk out of Grbavica unannounced, it would have been the same thing. This is what happens when you have a front line in a war zone. You can't just cross a front line in a war zone, Mr. Karadzic, not when people have guns there unannounced and say, "Oh, I just want to cross the other side." It doesn't work like that. It's an extremely dangerous thing to do. It's the basic rule for war correspondents. You don't cross sides. We did, and every time we did we got shot at. For the normal population to do this in such circumstances is unthinkable without it having been properly organised beforehand, usually with the intervention of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. van Lynden, that we asked for the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge to be opened for several hours a day for free passage to one side and the other and that that is the way it was, sometimes?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When such things would had been properly organised, then it would have been possible. I was never there when that happened, and I never filmed it. I've been at the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge. I was there with General Rose in March 1994. But I have never seen, "Okay, we'll just open the bridge and people can come backwards and forwards without any problem. That absolutely did not happen, in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to this document. A person has his own papers, documents, and he applies to leave but then he cannot leave. However, if he has the papers that a foreign journalist has, then he can leave. That's what time talking about, Mr. van Lynden. It's a question of papers, documents. That is to say that citizens of Sarajevo were not allowed to leave of their own accord and on the basis of their own documents, but they needed foreign documents in order to be able to leave. Isn't that right? This is a Muslim document.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that's been asked and answered completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When first asked, Mr. van Lynden said that he didn't understand the nature of the question, so now I think he put the question and he said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I can answer the question as far as -- firstly, I don't -- I haven't seen this document ever before. The second thing is that what you needed as a foreign journalist to get in and out were not papers from your own news organisation, but you needed to get a UN pass. For that you needed foreign documents. Only with a UN pass could you cross backwards and forwards. It's that UN pass that your forces on the one hand and the Bosnian forces on the other hand would want to see. With that we could, at our own risk, and it was risky every time we did it, we could go in and out of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Mr. van Lynden, that in London and during the Carrington Conference and later on in Geneva we -- well, rather under the mediation of Mrs. Sadako Ogata, the three parties signed an agreement on the right of civilians to move about freely provided that their trip is announced. Then they would get an escort, et cetera. Do you know that that was signed in accordance with the Geneva conventions and that that was supposed to be observed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of all sorts of things being signed, but they weren't always carried out in reality. I am aware that, for instance, in 1992 for the Barcelona Olympics a delegation from the Bosnian side, including two athletes, if I remember a woman runner and a male judo fighter, were allowed to leave under UN escort to the airport and then on a UN plane to, I imagine, first to Zagreb and then on to Barcelona. Therefore, it could be arranged, and, yes, via the United Nations with announcement and with agreement from both sides. Thinking back on and in relation to the document that you are showing to the Court at the moment, while I always brought producers with me, other organisations employed whilst in Sarajevo, interpreters, or producers who were locals, I am not aware of them taking those people ever outside of Sarajevo. They would have been given accreditation, but it would have been considered too dangerous to take someone like that outside of Sarajevo from one side of the front lines to the other side, because they would have been seen as either being a spy or whatever by the other side, and therefore, I'm not aware of -- it may have happened, but I'm not aware of any Western news organisation giving accreditation to a Bosnian and then getting them out of Sarajevo once that person had been given UN accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's the way it was on both sides; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a producer, for instance, Jaksa Scekic, in Belgrade, and he came out to Pale, but he never into Sarajevo. No, that was his personal wish. He thought that he might then be accused by the Bosnians of being a spy or whatever. So we did not do so. The two field producers that I generally used in Bosnia, one was Zoran Kusovac whose father is from Montenegro, his mother is from Dalmatia, and who was born in Bosnia, and therefore he is a Yugoslav who no longer has a nation, and he was considered as someone that I could take to all sides. And the other was a Hungarian Yugoslav from Novi Sad, Apat Nehmet [phoen]. He was also considered that I could take him to all sides, and we did. As I said, other organisations employed Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Muslims in -- in Sarajevo or in Pale to help them with their work, and it was generally not considered safe to bring those people to the other side of the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the document, well, I don't expect that you have seen the document. I am actually referring to a phenomenon here that you are aware of. Did you know that criminals made tons of money by transferring people, by getting them out of town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the rumours. I never saw proof while I was there, nor would I have been likely to. If this was a criminal endeavour, they would not have shown it to the world's cameras. I am aware that people were smuggled out of the city and whether the criminals were on one side or the other side or both sides making money out of smuggling people, I don't know. I think it's probably likely that they were making money on both sides on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, this report of the service of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to this one, Your Honour. The witness, when asked about it, when it was first read out to him, he was asked you know about that and he said no, and there is no nexus in -- that hasn't had any impeachment value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We agree. This will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may I just say that Mr. van Lynden confirmed the existence of the phenomenon. He confirmed that he had heard had of such things, that people could not leave town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about this document. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he won't be able to say anything about any document, because I'm not asking him about documents. I'm asking him about phenomena, occurrences, events. He could not have seen these documents. These were documents of the Muslim Secret Service, the military secret service at that. Anyway, let's move on. 1D01228.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this -- ah, it's here. Mr. van Lynden, do you know that citizens could orient themselves on the basis of whether TV crews were there or not? They would expect something to happen, something bad to happen, when they'd see foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign journalists tend to come to places when something bad is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unless they know in advance that something is going to happen; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't. Practically never, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document again of the Muslim army. Yet again it's the security administration. Can we have page three now. "Reliable sources," that's -- ah, yes, right. Here it is. I'm going to read it out in Serbian. "A reliable source of the military security service of the 1st Corps who is close to the CNN news team observed that lately there has been a greater presence of foreign media representatives in Sarajevo. It was especially noticed that news teams are primarily composed of more experienced war zone reporters who also reported on the Gulf War and who would not have come to Sarajevo unless they expected that 'something important was about to happen.'" That was under quotation marks. "The source also relayed the information provided by one member of the CNN team that 'some' rushed preparations are being observed in the NATO bases in Germany as well," the "some" was under quotation marks, "which can be seen from the higher transportation of soldiers and equipment as well as flights." What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have not seen this document before, and I should also states that in my opinion if I had been shown these documents before I could maybe give -- would have been able to give you a more thought-through answer, but my instant reaction to this is that this is probably a bit of Bosnian wishful thinking. We encountered it throughout the war, that certain Bosnians would say to us, ah, this and this is happening, which probably wasn't, or that -- I don't know where they'd heard it from, in the hope of military intervention by NATO. And as far as I'm aware in August nothing was undertaken by NATO. The only thing that happened was a conference in London that did not help end the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that refused to take part in that conference bona fide? Let me be more precise. Did you know that Izetbegovic said that Silajdzic would go there but not to negotiate, rather, to express his dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, Mr. Izetbegovic went to the conference himself. I recall meeting him there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This has to do with 1993. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, in the same manner. The witness didn't say anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think he can say anything about secret documents. It says here, "Military secret," high --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we gave our ruling. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in the future. What will I do with documents that witnesses had not seen before, but I would like the witnesses to state their views on particular phenomena rather than actual documents. Can I ask them about phenomena, occurrences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked the question, and you got his answer. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see General Rose's book?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it in a bookstore, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you something from that book if you just saw it in a bookstore, if you hadn't read it actually?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did have meetings with General Rose, and you received information from him. So --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any information from General Rose. I did have a couple of meetings with him and one interview with -- in front of the television camera, but I never got any information from General Rose, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did receive information from persons who were under his command, right, his people?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did get information during 1994 when General Rose was in Bosnia from various elements of the -- of UNPROFOR, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about 1992? You didn't receive any information from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not from General Rose because he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1037. Could I have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're we are waiting for that, I'm not talking about General Rose in personal terms. I'm talking about UNPROFOR, the united nations, the military wing of the United Nations, that you received information from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1037. And then could we have -- yes. It is page 243 and 244. Page 243 and then page 244 of the book, this book, that is. That's the number of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page, "My own theory." Do you see that bit, "My own theory of this misrepresentation." "[In English] My own theory at this misrepresentation of the truth did little to stem the tide of propaganda. The perception of many US east coast commentators is that during the fighting in Gorazde in the UN -- the UN deliberately misled the world about what happened, underestimated the scale of the disaster, and was economical with the truth. I explained that most of the damages -- damaged houses in Gorazde revealed by US air reconnaissance had not been destroyed in the fighting and took -- that took place in this -- in the town in April 1994. They had been destroyed in 1992 when the Muslims drove the Serbs from the town and surrounding area. These former Serb homes had no roofs, window frames, or doors, and had been stripped of all furniture and fitting -- fittings. Many of them had been tortured -- torched. They were demonstrably not buildings recently subjected to shelling. Today, the UN still stands condemned for having underplayed the damage done by the Serbs in Gorazde." [Interpretation] As you reported about Gorazde, did you know how the Serbs had fared in Gorazde in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was first in Gorazde at the beginning of 1993, in February, beginning of March. We met Serbs living there, including and going to one small village which was entirely populated by Serbs. So precisely what occurred in the spring of 1992 in Gorazde, I don't know and I didn't see with my own eyes. There was clearly fighting there as there was in the whole of Eastern Bosnia, and clearly many people from other areas of Eastern Bosnia who had been forced by your forces to flee their homes and their villages and their towns had moved into Gorazde, and there had been fighting there as well. But to the precise nature of what happened to the buildings that General Rose is referring to, I don't know. I don't think that General Rose was in Gorazde in 1992, either, so I don't think he knows. What I do know in relation to Gorazde of 1994, which he refers to, is when we met General Rose in March 1994 in Sarajevo after having been in Pale, we informed him that we had had information while in Pale that Gorazde would be attacked by the forces under General Mladic in April 1994. General Rose's reaction at that time was that how could we know such a thing and that we were wrong, and we said we did not know for certain but that we had spoken to certain people while we were in Pale to had warned us that this was going to happen. As far as I can judge, General Rose didn't bear that warning from us, and pretty unfortunate circumstances arose in April 1994, including the loss of life of one of General Rose's personal soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you mean to say is that the military secret of Mladic's army was something that you could hear around the streets of Pale, these military secrets going round?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were wary with the information. One always is. You get to hear a lot of rumours if you're a journalist in a war zone, and much of the rumour is incorrect. We had heard, not on the streets but from, let's say, more informed contacts that specifically Jaksa Scekic had built up there that an attack on Gorazde by General Mladic was likely in April, and we simply passed that on to General Rose and were slightly surprised by his reaction at the time, because he dismissed it out of hand, which of course it's his right to do, but as it turned out, we were right and the information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me when the Serb army attacks Gorazde with an offensive that it wasn't a counter-offensive? When did the Serb -- when was it that the Serb army attacked Gorazde without any provocation from Gorazde? Quote me a single example if you can.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear, Mr. Karadzic, that for you everything is only ever a counter-offensive. No one ever shot at the Bosnians until the Bosnians shot at the Serbs. I'm sure that there were instances where the Bosnians did shoot first, leading to a counter-attack. Was I in Gorazde at that time? No, I wasn't. Is the information that I've just given to this Court correct that we were told in Pale in March 1994 that an attack was likely in April on Gorazde, yes, that information is correct, and did such an attack occur? Yes, it did. Can I say absolutely that it's the whole truth and nothing but the truth that this was not to a degree a counter-offensive? No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, were you in Eastern Bosnia and did you see with your very own eyes how my forces -- did you see my forces expelling Muslims from their houses and sending them away from Gorazde, expelling them? Did you ever see that with your very own eyes?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Gorazde, no, because Gorazde remained an enclave that held out. We went through various other places where houses had been torched, villages that were empty. We met people who had been forced to flee from villages and towns right across Eastern Bosnia. When we were in Gorazde, we met a lot of these people who were living in schools or wherever else they could who were refugees from other areas. Did I actually see it myself? No, I wasn't in Bosnia in March, April, May 1992, but this is what we always heard and others did witness. For instance, in Bijeljina, Ron Aviv [phoen] saw it happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said a moment ago that in Gorazde there were people who were expelled by my forces as if you'd seen it yourself.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did meet the people, yes, and that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, they said that, but you don't know that for a fact. You have no other proof and evidence apart from what they told you; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have proof and evidence that they were living as refugees in Gorazde, where the population had certainly tripled from what it was before the war. And it was confirmed by everyone there, including by the Serbs who were living inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were there Serbs living within the enclave in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already testified there were. There was at least one village where we were taken, including a man who actually had a firm in Rotterdam and with whom I was able to speak in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you saw him in Serb Gorazde, that is say the Serbian part of Gorazde, not the Muslim part; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met him within the enclave controlled by the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the beginning of 1993, were you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that and deal with that later on, but may we have 1D982 next, please. This excerpt from General Rose's book, can I tender it into evidence, where he writes about how foreign journalists report on the situation showing Serb houses to be Muslim houses and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me. I don't see that -- I can't see that reference, but I don't object to this page we've just been looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 174 was previously admitted, but the Bench will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness said nothing about the book, so we'll not admit that part of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know what happened in Gorazde in 1994?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the entire year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time you were -- at the time you asked about Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Gorazde in -- for a couple of weeks in March 1993, and I have never returned to Gorazde after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what period did you alert Rose to? 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but then I left Bosnia, and I was actually in Belgrade when the offensives, whomever may have launched them initially, took place at Gorazde, and it was at that period that I received a letter from the Yugoslav authorities telling me that I was persona non grata and that I had to leave the country, and so I 48 hours to leave Belgrade and return to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I hear of anything like that, Mr. van Lynden. All the Serb presidents received you for interviews and dinners after interviews, and suddenly in 1994 you say you became persona non grata. How do you explain that? [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For life, Mr. Karadzic. I think I can go back to Serbia now. I don't think Mr. Milosevic can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you had that kind of approach and access, whereas we received bias reports from you. So we couldn't have won the media war, because you had access wherever you wanted to. President Milosevic, President Karadzic, you could go there officially and privately, but we achieved nothing with you. So that is why 1994 you deserved being considered that you were detrimental to their state interests in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion. No. I just absolutely disagree with that. I think it was important that international correspondents were given access, and throwing journalists out is not the right response and only damages those who do the throwing out. I don't think this is the place to have a debate as to Serbian policy with the foreign media. I personally believe it to be very mistaken from the beginning. And what you stated earlier of me being -- having private access to Mr. Milosevic is utter nonsense. I met him once. I did an interview. He invited me for one drink afterwards and that was it. I never had dinner with you, as far as I can recall. I was invited for drinks on several occasions. I was once invited by General Mladic for lunch. That is the sum total. In other parts of the world I've had more access, far more access, with the leaders of the countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now things are much clearer. Now, let's turn to page 6 of this report, please, by General Janvier. Can we go down to "Similar." "Similar to what happened." "[In English] Similar to what happened in Gorazde (spring 94) the BiH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR (including the rapid reaction forces) of NATO into the conflict on the BiH side. Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave, or alarming reports from Bosnian side on the situation in the enclaves, will be indicators for this. A stronger involvement of the international community would be interpreted by the Bosnian Serb Army as an incentive to step up operations and try to eliminate the enclave, as well as retaliate against the UN forces. "Based on the tank firings that occurred at Zepa yesterday, similar BSA efforts at Zepa could occur in the next few days." [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. van Lynden, you see that General Janvier is reporting here about the trickery, the tricks, that took place in Gorazde, with the stage collapse of the lines, the infiltration of the United Nations into the conflict, throwing out UN soldiers, and then once they withdraw, they remain in an encirclement of ours. Now, do you see what was going on in Gorazde when you were there? And it's the event that you draw Rose's attention to; right? Warned him about it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there. When I was there in March 1993, there was actually almost no fighting going on whatsoever. There was a lot of snow. What we had warned General Rose about in March 1994 was that what we had been told while we were in Pale. We know that fighting took place at April 1994 around the Gorazde enclave. That we can agree. Do I know the precise nature of that fighting? No, I wasn't there at the time. My only -- I cannot react to what -- Janvier is saying this for reasons best known to General Janvier. The one enclave I was in in 1994 was the Bihac enclave which, and I spent several weeks there, and I saw with my own eyes that that enclave was attacked not only from within Bosnia but also by Serb forces in Croatia across the line that the UN was meant to stop them from doing so and the UN did nothing. That I know because there I was and I saw it. I wasn't there in Gorazde in the spring of 1994. The only thing I testified to this Court was that in March I told General Rose what we had been told in Pale. Given the fact that there was fighting in the Gorazde enclave in April 1994, I don't think that information was completely wrong, although I don't know the precise nature of the beginning of that fighting, which is what you're alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But General Janvier is reporting about the same thing, and he says that there were tricks to involve the UN forces or NATO in Gorazde. So you say that you heard about this from someone in Pale, although I doubt that anybody knew Mladic's plans at the time or that he had any plans to attack Gorazde for that matter. Now, what about Bihac? Is that the full truth, or is the truth of it that from Bihac they took about 300 square kilometres and almost reached Bosanski Brod which was purely Serb territory, and then in a counter-offensive General Milovanovic managed to return it to the enclave? Do you know that before that that they -- the Muslims had arrived at almost Bosanski Petrovac, that line from the protected area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a war both sides launch offensives, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, you have represented it as the Serbs attacking Bihac. The Serbs, first of all, had to liberate 300 square kilometres or even more territory, to liberate it and then to reach the outskirts of Bihac through a counter-offensive. That's what it's about. And we see what General Janvier says about that. Now, are you challenging the observations made by General Janvier here?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can absolutely not confirm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you challenge them then? Do you believe what he says or not, or do you disbelieve it? Can -- is General Janvier somebody who can be believed or not?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was with the Bosnian forces in Bihac, and you're right that there was a counter-offensive by the Serb, but there was also a counter-offensive from Croatia which was meant to be a UN protected area, and that was not meant to happen. I have not witnessed the Bosnian forces behaving in the manner described by General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do we agree that the Serb forces from Croatia were in Abdic's campaign and not campaigning of their own accord? And was Abdic at war with the Bihac 5th Corps at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abdic was up in Velika Kladusa, but there were attacks also from other areas in which the Croatian Serb forces became involved. Two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, the forces of the Croatian Serbs were in an alliance with Abdic. So they didn't go to Bihac for themselves, but Abdic laid down the right to have Bihac and that whole enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Serbs were part of a UN protected zone and were coming across an international border and should not have been allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is already an exhibit, so I'm not going to tender it now, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we be informed of the exhibit number of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was admitted as Exhibit D137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have some more time before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break, after which you will have three-quarters of an hour, Mr. Karadzic. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have 1D1037. It's Rose's book. We were looking at it earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. van Lynden, let me tell you why this is important for me. We had a witness here who said -- well, he made some assertions, and when -- yes. Can I have page 54 of this book. But when I asked him, the witness, how he knew about that he said, "Well, it's common knowledge, generally accepted." So public opinion crops up as proof and evidence as a document. Now let's see how General Rose views this, and let's turn to page 54 for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I was beginning," that paragraph. "[In English] I was beginning to be able to distinguish between those journalists who unquestionably used material provided by the Bosnian government propaganda machine and those who were interested in presenting a more objective view of the war. Much seemed to depend on individual personalities and what sort of relationship the reporters had developed with the female interpreters attached to all foreign news teams by the Bosnian government. Not all the journalists in Sarajevo were biased, and I worked with many courageous reporters who often put their own lives at risk in order to discover the truth. Kurt Schork, an American who had been at Oxford with President Clinton and worked for Reuters, and Remy Ourdan, a Breton who reported for "Le Monde," were two such people. A television news clip once showed Kurt running out from under cover and heavy mortar fire to pull a wounded woman to safety." [Interpretation] And so on. Therefore -- therefore, Mr. van Lynden, wouldn't it be nice if on this list we were to find the Sky News team?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's an observation, not a question. A rhetorical question. I'm sure the witness would be jolly pleased to see the Sky News team on a list depending on what the list said. But this is obviously simply the individual subjective view of the author of the book, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Excellency, he was the commander, the United Nations commander, and he has this ongoing criticism saying reporting from the area was being done erroneously to the detriment of the Serbs, and then he quotes these two courageous people and unbiased people, but the Prosecution did not call those two people into court here. And on the other hand, I think that Sky News would have liked to find itself on this list of unbiased people and courageous people, but my question is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].'

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you accept that large number of journalists - let's leave Sky News aside for a moment - that they were furnished with news by the Presidency, information from the Presidency? Now, you didn't have a female interpreter that the Presidency provided you with, but others did. So do you agree that the use of information predominantly from the Presidency was biased and one-sided?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in my opinion, and I have not read this book as I have already testified, the line that General Rose uses, "what sort of relationship the reporters had developed with the female interpreters attached to all foreign news teams by the Bosnian government," that line should have warned you not to use such things. It's a -- firstly, it's absolutely not true, and General Rose might have known that. The assertion in the line that basically all the foreign correspondents were being charmed by Bosnian young ladies at the instigation of the Bosnian government, that's within this line, is a terrible one and again is not true, and you should -- you should have been warned by that. Secondly, your assertion that Kurt Schork, who was killed ten years ago, should be a witness at this Tribunal I find fairly shocking. You should also note, Your Honours, that a street in Sarajevo is named after Kurt Schork, who was very critical of the Bosnian Serbs and was also critical of the UN and who was a great personal friend of mine. We often worked together. I think that's really all I want to say about this piece from Mr. Rose's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Rose says that he could distinguish between two types of journalists. So there were both sorts. Now may we look at page 69 and 70, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just say to that there were many more than just two sorts. The world is more complicated than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, if I remember rightly and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, wasn't Kurt Schork later killed reporting in Sierra Leone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Many journalists [Interpretation] Let's look for the paragraph beginning with "Many journalists." On page 69, towards the bottom, I believe. "[In English] Many journalists -- many journalists in Sarajevo also supported the war option, either because they believed that it was morally right to engage in some form of holy war against the Serbs or else because images of war -- images of war sell better than those of peace. A journalist working for a leading London newspaper summed up this view when he told Simon Shadbolt that he did not care about the facts or the UN arguments in favour of peace, his object was to get the West involved in a war in Bosnia." [Interpretation] Do you believe that there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not believe that any journalist that I ever encountered in Bosnia believed in any kind of holy war against the Serbs. That's something in the Serb figment of the imagination. That's utter nonsense. And an unnamed journalist working for a leading London newspaper, I'm surprised General Rose could write such things. I really cannot comment further on that. I'm pretty outraged to read something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would be surprised if he had written that nothing like that existed. It obviously existed and so General Rose took that position and view; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection to the comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a comment. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't it right that Rose wouldn't have written that had that not existed? Why would Rose have written this paragraph if that's not how things were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to comment upon the mind of Mr. Rose. Let's not move on to another topic of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these pages be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I wonder if you might consider that a little bit longer. I think that this was -- it's particularly the first passage. There was something that was within the knowledge of Mr. van Lynden concerning the foreign journalists and how they were treated by the Bosnian government. He spoke to that. It was not consistent with General Rose, but nevertheless he spoke to that, and I think under your most resent guidelines this is at least a closer question and in my view should be admissible. I would note also that General Rose is coming as a witness in this case for the Prosecution, which would make it more useful for the Chamber to have this material before it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, that's going to be the occasion for whatever General Rose testifies about. If he wishes to align that to material contained in his book, he'll be free to adduce that as being something inconsistent with the testimony he's going to give. But what in fact Mr. van Lynden did was to state his own views and not adopt the views that were contained in the book. So it seems to me that under whatever policy one uses for the admission of documents, this is still not a document which has been adopted by the witness. In fact, Mr. van Lynden went out of his way to disassociate himself with the document in general and parts of it in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There was a unanimous decision of the Chamber. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, 1D1294.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document, Mr. van Lynden, I would like to inform you why it is that I want to put these things before you. You said that the Green Berets are a figment of the Serbs' imagination. You also said that other things had to do with imagination as far as the Serbs were concerned, namely that the Muslims were inflicting harm on themselves. You did admit that the Serbs were misportrayed a bit in the media. But anyway, let's see what the conditions were. Under which conditions were we waging war and under which conditions are these -- these proceedings taking place, and to what extent was I satanised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, one, it's a large compound question, but for this question I would request that the guidelines be followed and I be given cites to the testimony. I'd like to know which portions of the direct or earlier cross Mr. Karadzic is referring to if he knows. If he has no cites whatsoever, then I'll allow this to keep moving on, but if he is knows what parts he's talking about, I'd like to know which pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you said that the witness admitted Serbs were misportrayed a bit in the media. Could you direct our attention to what portion you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that the -- the Muslims were harming themselves was a figment of imagination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation, Excellency. Now, this is the way it is: During his interview with me and while he testified here Mr. van Lynden said that he had not seen the Green Berets and that the Green Berets were a figment of the Serbs' imagination. Whereas in the interview he said to me, and he confirmed that here, that the weakest point of our defence is the claim that the Muslims fired at their own people. We have all of that on the record. We heard all of that in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have page 7519. 1D007519. Page 6 if you count them. 7514 is the first one, so we need 7519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what book this is about? Who authored this? Who compiled this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a book that was compiled by Zoran Petrovic, Piro Canac [phoen], Vesna Hadzivuckovic [phoen], and Tomislav Kresovic. It was published in 1994; that is to say, it was up until 1994 that the attitude of the foreign media was analysed. I mean, vis-a-vis the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we lower this? Can we scroll down so that we see the picture that was in the "Chicago Tribune."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this, Mr. van Lynden. Serbs are these pigs and the Russians are those other pigs, although it says "Commies" in all fairness. How would this affect the public opinion in America?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not very much, because it didn't seem to change American policy as far as I could judge. I see it's the 1st of January, 1993. As far as I'm aware, the American military intervention, when it did take place, was in August 1995. And I can't really comment on the effect of -- on a whole nation by one cartoon in one newspaper in the United States, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this fair reporting, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not reporting, Mr. Karadzic. It's a cartoon. If you look at the cartoons, there was a famous cartoonist working for Vreme. Is that anti-Serb as well? I believe he was a Serb. I believe he was pretty effective with his cartoons, certainly for the Serb population as to what he was doing. I mean, you could put his cartoons there and you could ask the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 7538. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up here we see it says "Muslims slaughter their own people." However -- actually, we are not going to deal with that now. We saw it elsewhere. Let's look at the photograph down here. Could we have the lower part of the page, the photograph. This is what we discussed: "[In English] I saw a TV camera crew and an ambulance standing nearby, half an hour before. Everything was stage managed." [Interpretation] This is Vasa Miskin street or, rather, the bread line. What I have put to you already, Mr. van Lynden, this is a lady obviously from Sarajevo. There is this belief in Sarajevo: When you see foreign journalist, run. Do you believe that now when you see this statement made by this Muslim lady as to what it was that had happened there, namely that the media had been informed in advance as to what would happen?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been informed in advance as to what will happen. We were never taken to a position and told something's going to happen here for you to film. I have never been told by any of my colleagues of that. So, no. I mean, neither side or any of the three sides, no one ever took me anywhere beforehand and said something is going to happen for you to film. No. I am totally unaware of that. I am completely unaware of any crew being taken anywhere either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 7564 now, please. Mr. van Lynden, did you ever mention rape in your reports, the Serb campaign of raping Muslim women as a war strategy -- or, rather, a means employed in war?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did towards the end of 1992 report and interview various women to this who told us what had happened to them, that they had been held, some for weeks, some for even longer, and been raped. Did we mention that this was a strategy of war? No, we did not until the full size of this operation was revealed in UN and EU studies. As a lone correspondent working in a war zone, you -- you -- lone - that's in single for the translation, "l-o-n-e," not "alone" - you don't have the resources to go around interviewing everyone, but when the reports come out by the EU and the UN saying that tens of thousands of women had been raped and that in the opinion of those who put the reports together this had been a strategy of war, yes, quoting those documents we did report that. But that's later in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this, what it says here. "[In English] There is no evidence such camps exist or ever existed. Philippe Misery, official of the International Red Cross. [Interpretation] That's what he said in relation to these camps. Once the story about the death camps would not hold water, then it was rape camps that were launched, and the figure that was used was even up to 60.000; right? 60.000 was referred to most often, but the figure actually went up to 80.000; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard people go up to 80.000, yes, but as far as I can recall, that is not the figure that was used in the EU and UN reports. Did we actually report on rape camps? No, we did not. Was I ever taken to one? No, I was not. The figures as I remember them from the UN and EU reports talked of figures of over 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know ultimately how many raped women there were? Muslim women that were raped. I'm not referring to Serb women now. Muslim women that were raped. How many they ultimately found. How many cases were actually confirmed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that it's a two-digit figure?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only in later reports basing myself on the reports of the EU and the UN reported that this had happened to somewhere around 20.000 women, possibly more, because that's what those reports put together by large teams of people claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these reports did not actually stand for long?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 7579. Could we have that now, please. Sorry, first 7583. 7583 first. Of this book that is. While we're waiting, Mr. van Lynden, did you know how many prisons there were for Serbs in Sarajevo, and did you know about the Serbs, the thousands of Serbs, who were detained at the Kosevo stadium?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We asked for figures, and we asked to be taken to prisons in Sarajevo. I never was. I was taken to a prison in Gorazde, and I was taken to a prison in Bihac where we were able to speak to the prisoners, but I was never given the opportunity to speak to the prisoners held within Sarajevo, nor was I ever given a figure of how many people were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you disputing the fact that there were 127 prisons in Sarajevo, many of which were private prisons where Serbs were held as slaves?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position either to confirm or to dispute those. I'm simply saying I did not know. We asked, and I wasn't told, and I wasn't brought to any of those prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if that were to be proven to be true, would you think that the Muslim government had deceived you and put you in a position not to know about 127 prisons and not to know about thousands of Serbs being detained in Kosevo stadium? Do you think that this was a very serious matter that you did not report on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all war zones one tries as best one can to see as many prisoners and to film as many prisoners as possible. Also to a degree to do them a personal service. If you film someone still alive, it makes it much harder for whatever side in a war zone to kill them. We tried to do that in Sarajevo. I personally did not succeed, and that is all I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at this page. This is how "The Independent" saw us on the 29th of May, 1992, how we were portrayed. What you see here, does that correspond to your experience with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 7 -- 7579, rather. Mr. van Lynden, you reported about the humanitarian situation there and the like; right? Could you please cast a glance at this. "[In English] Humanitarian aid delivered by road through a corridor across Serbian territories from April the 1st to 23rd of August, 1993." [Interpretation] Do you see that? Muslims got nine times more flour than the Serbs did. Biscuits, 100 per cent more. Sugar, 26 times more. Then cooking oil, 74 tonnes. The Serbs didn't get any. And so on and so forth. So what does this look like to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything about what the Serbs got or -- oh, I see now what you're referring to. I imagine this is a reference to UNHCR aid, and if it's an UNHCR document, I do not dispute it. I don't know if it's right or wrong. What I would say is that on the one hand a besieged enclave was being fed because it was its only source of sustenance was largely food brought from the outside, and then on the other side of the front line it's a different situation. There were farms and openings for the Bosnian Serbs to get food through the normal manners. And I suspect that you would have to get someone from the UNHCR who is an expert on this kind of thing to answer your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
