utterances.text: Could we scroll down a bit. Mr. van Lynden, you know, that Serbia was under sanctions and we could only trade with Serbia. After that, Republika Srpska was under sanctions as well, even sanctions imposed by Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that the Republika Srpska was under sanctions imposed by Yugoslavia. Indeed, we filmed -- after Mr. Milosevic had announced those sanctions we filmed those sanctions being broken, specifically as far as petrol and oil was concerned. Yes, there were sanctions for Serbia imposed by the UN, but these were regularly broken. All sides, from Macedonia, from Romania, from Bulgaria, something that we also filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to this -- actually, we have to go into closed session. Can we have 1D02182. We are going to be in closed session very briefly. 1282, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you showed four or five pictures or clippings from that book, but I'm not satisfied with the relevance of the first one, and then the -- as to the remaining one, we were not provided with the foundation evidence, and the witness was not able to confirm anything about it, and in relation to the bread queue, we already admitted "The Independent" clipping, but as to the picture, we're not satisfied with this foundation. For those reasons, we are not minded to admit them at all. You will have another opportunity to introduce those documents if we are satisfied with its relevance. Final questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My final question is this: Mr. van Lynden, we heard from you that you consider that we are responsible for not informing the world sufficiently about our situation, put our case to the world. Now, do you consider that the media nonetheless did inflict a great deal of damage to the Serbs regardless of whether we were to blame or whether the media were to blame? Do you -- do you think that it was unjustified and that the picture that went out into the world about our image was far blacker than it need have been and should have been?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking for my impression, Mr. Karadzic, and you had said when I was here first that you didn't want my impressions. I believe that the Serbs indeed are responsible for the image that they received during the war in Bosnia, in the Western media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that that image did not reflect the actual state of affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that I believe that the Serbs are responsible for the image that they received during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. van Lynden. A very small point but I want to clear it up. Mr. Karadzic today at page 28, lines 1 to 10, implied that this was the first time today that you had ever said, spoken about how in April 1994 you were told to leave Belgrade for life. Do you recall speaking about that during your cross-examination in the Slobodan Milosevic case, 16 September 2003, at transcript page 26764? There you stated in April 1994, continuing: "It was my last days in Serbia because then I was then ordered to leave the country after your government decided to call me persona non grata for life." Do you recall that you spoke about that indent back in 2003 under oath?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that you also discussed that in the Martic case and in the Perisic cases?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to go now to some questioning by Mr. Karadzic about front lines. You were cross-examined about video P936. That's the video from 5th December 1992 of the apartment building burning where the incendiary bullet bounces nearby you and your cameraman, and you were questioned about a statement in that report that the building was a civilian target, and you were asked this question on the 21st of May, this is at 2628, line 18. Mr. Karadzic said: "Thank you. In another video-clip you said that the defenders had turned apartments and offices into places" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- "from where there was shooting and that explains what just -- what you said just now and I'll accept it." And your answer was: "No, no, no. No, no. Wait a second. On the front lines, as also on your side of the front lines, apartments and office blocks were turned into military installations. This was not a front line apartment building. This was a civilian apartment building that was targeted. Quite different to the other positions on the -- right on the front lines." What I'd like to do is play just part of the clip that Mr. Karadzic cited in support of his question to you. That's 40264B is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Van Lynden: Stark evidence of another night of fierce shelling in a city that's gradually being destroyed. Close by lie the front lines of an urban war, offices and homes turned into machine-gun emplacements by the defenders of Sarajevo. Their Serb foes are close, very close. This burnt out tank just 80 yards away. Hidden around the city's Jewish cemetery are other Serb positions, a district of town where the guns are rarely quiet."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's stop there at 04:47:6. Now, the front line positions, the offices and buildings turned into machine-gun nests that you talked about in this story that Mr. Karadzic quoted, where were they located?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were located on the Bosnian side of the front line by the Miljacka River just opposite the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The burning apartment building we saw in the story from December 5th, 1992, where was that building located approximately?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- we're in the western part of the town, fairly close to the television station. It's a completely different part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Did that building have anything to do, the one that we saw burning in the December 5th, 1992, film, did that have anything to do with the clip Mr. Karadzic referred to about the front lines?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were completely separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked also on the 21st of May, this is at 2595, line 14, by Mr. Karadzic, continuing on to 2597, about damage to the former military hospital or city hospital when you entered it, and Mr. Karadzic characterised it as being pocked marked and there was some questioning about the nature of the damage. I'd like to play continuing from this same 65 ter number, another portion starting at 6:15 approximately. If you could watch this, please. And I should say this is from June 3rd, this news story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Sarajevo city hospital provides graphic proof, an incongruous target that's been hit every single day."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We're at 06:29:3. Could you just tell us which building is this that we've stopped on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the former military hospital. The building that we've stayed in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- spent a lot of time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Play it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Unscathed by shrapnel or bullet. For the brooms of the cleaners, an almost hopeless task. It was once a military hospital, but the lieutenant-colonel who left in such a hurry that his uniform still hang on their pegs would hardly recognise it now. Across the corridor the office of a colleague has simply disappeared. Yet the hospital still functions. Its intensive care unit fully operational."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can stop. Thank you. Stopped at 06:59:5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very simply, that video that was broadcast on June 3rd, does it fairly and accurately reflect the condition of the hospital when you stayed there in early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it shows only a small part of the damage that it had sustained. I mean, it was -- the damage was really huge already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask to admit that story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the 65 ter number again please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was 40264B.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something? Parts of the interior, the shots of the interior, are they of the military hospital as well, or was that filmed somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're not allowed to ask questions during the redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whether I'm going to object to it's -- being admitted or not depends on the answer I'm given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, can you assist on the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of that was filmed at the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that explanation, we'll admit the part of the film.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P954, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you some questions arising from the cross-examination where you were continually accused on your earlier cross-examination and again today of bias, both yourself and the media in general. Principally you've been accused of reporting on Serb -- not reporting on Serb losses and the existence of fire from Muslim positions at Serb positions amongst other things. Specifically, 20th of May at 2522 Mr. Karadzic said that all of your reports and the reports of many of your colleagues do not leave any doubt in anybody's mind as to the Serbs being the ones to attack, and it's always their fault. At 2451, line 1, on 19th of May, Mr. Karadzic put it to you that your reports showed that nobody was actually shooting at the Serbs and that the city was unarmed without any artillery, without any soldiers, without any actions going on. And the Serbs without having suffered any losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now play P806, please, in response to those questions, and I'll have a couple questions. Your Honours, this is referenced in paragraphs 101 and 104 of the amalgamated statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Van Lynden: The Serb position is a commanding one. They have the whole of Sarajevo in their sights, with tree tops shorn to provide better fields of fire. The slopes are practically insurmountable to direct attack and the lines of sturdy log cabins, some already being prepared for winter, have an air of permanence. For the moment, the Serb guardians of these hilltop strongholds appear relaxed, yet they're adamant that anything won in battle cannot be surrendered in negotiation. "Soldier: Giving any territory away would be a great treason against their people and the Serb capitulation. "Van Lynden: In Grbavica, the only district of central Sarajevo the Serbs control, that opinion was shared by all the soldiers, even if many of these elderly civilians congregating to collect their pensions are Muslims. The war having halted earlier payments, now they received their allotted share for April and May. It's meager, between 3 and 8 pounds per person, which cannot buy a lot in an adjacent shop plentiful by Sarajevo standards. Then the calm of the morning is shattered by a sniper's bullet. A woman is hit, and the 20-millimetre gun of an APC fires a concerted repast. "The threat of the sniper forces any approach to the front lines to be made crouched and at speed. Here the guns are seldom silent. "Neither the London Conference, with all it's stated promises and principles, nor the continuing talks in Geneva, would appear to have made one jot of difference here. The shooting and siege continue, just as they have done for the past five months. Much of the front line that divides Grbavica from the rest of Sarajevo is a natural one. The river Miljacka, its bridges watched continually from apartment block machine-gun nests. One gun, manned by an obese decoy. Here, as on the hillside, the mood is an uncompromising one. "Soldier: We are against it, we are against any concessions. "Soldier: It could have been resolved politically before, but not anymore. Now only militarily, until victory. "Van Lynden: Yet at rare times, even here there is compassion, a solitary Muslim woman allowed to cross the river in safety, freeing her from Serb control, but leaving her in a city besieged by them. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo. Aernout Van Lynden, Fox News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We stopped at the end -- we stopped at the end of the clip, the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when did you film and report on this story from the Serb side in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this after the interview with General Mladic where you asked for permission to visit different positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, just to be very clear for the record, when you're reporting there on sniping coming into Grbavica and a woman being hit, although we didn't see that on the film, which side is that, the Muslim or the Serb side that you were reporting on, sniper fire coming into and hitting women?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And very quickly to conclude. You were also asked on 20th of May, at 2557, line 10: "Q. If I tell you that foreign correspondents had no interest at all in the Serb side of the story, what do you say to that?" And you said that you're talking utter nonsense. We went to Pale and continued. And you went on to say: "When we were there in September, we were taken to a front line position outside Hadzici, a Serb-held position, and it came under fire. We filmed it and reported on it." And I want to show P808, if we may, Your Honour. This is in reference in paragraph 101 of the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Some duck for cover, others scramble to respond. For the Serb fighters on the hills west of Sarajevo, skirmishes like this one are sudden but daily fact of life. The forests resound to gunfire as local commanders with some urgency ask for more information. Even if the dense undergrowth limits their fields of fire, they take few risks, pouring pre-emptive machine-gun bursts down the slopes. "Soldier: For the past 15 days there's been heavy fighting here. Five of my men have died, 15 have been wounded. "Van Lynden: As ever, the Serbs hold the high ground, looking down on the Muslim villages in the valleys below. The Serbs took these hills two months ago and know that the Bosnian government forces must retake them if the ever worsening siege of Sarajevo is to be broken. "It's in the constant offensives and counter-offensives on fronts like this one, the demilitarisation of Sarajevo and the region that surrounds it is likely to break down even if the rival Bosnian leaders put their signatures to an agreement. "Certainly in the hillside trenches and bunkers we found no expectations of an early peace. Just a blind commitment to war. Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, on the front lines west of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is that the story you were referring to in your answer - I'm not sure - when you --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is outside Hadzici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in that story we saw that you reported that the Serb soldiers there had suffered casualties, 15 wounded, five dead according to --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That's the commander saying that. I didn't see the dead or the wounded, but that's what he told us, and we broadcast what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you also broadcast there that the Serb position was responding to fire and that there were constant offences and counter offences at fronts like that one. Why did you include that in the report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was the way it was. While we were there, that position came under fire, and there was a response from those soldiers to the incoming fire. That's what we filmed, and that's what we experienced, and that's what we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll play just one last one. If we could play P810, please. It's a short clip of the funeral in Vlasenica. It is referenced on page 113 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "In the eastern Bosnian town of Vlasenica, the bells of the Orthodox church toll for the dead, twenty-eight of them. They lie in simple pine coffins surrounded by the leaders of the Serbs, by relatives, and by almost the entire population of the town. The men, all Serb soldiers, were killed when their position was overrun last Saturday by Muslim forces. Only a date later were they found, their bodies horrifically mutilated, two even having been roasted on a spit, and the coffins could not hide the stench of defiled death from any bystander. "In slow procession they wind their way to the cemetery where the victims of Bosnia's last war lie. A new mass grave has been dug amongst the old, and here the latest victims of this new and barbarous war in Bosnia are laid down side by side. Colleagues fire a last salute and then leave the grave to parents, wives, and children unwilling to let the dead fall from their grasp. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Vlasenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. That's one of your reports referenced in your statement that you sent out, and I think it speaks for itself. You state in your statement at paragraph 113 that 28 soldiers were buried in that mass funeral which you covered. And you were also questioned a lot about government manipulation of the media and the way politicians manipulate the media, try to manipulate the media. Do you recall meeting with Mr. Karadzic at around this time and what he told you that who the victims were of this attack?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We met Mr. Karadzic, as I recall, before going there for the funeral and that he gave figures that several hundred people had been killed and that they were civilians. At the -- in Vlasenica we asked who these people were and they said to us that they were soldiers and there were 28 coffins, because we counted them, and the day after that we actually went to the position where these men had died and met their company commander who confirmed that it was 28 men who had died there and that no civilians had been killed in that particular attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. That concludes your evidence. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. I would, with your allowance, like to make a short statement about the rights of witnesses which I believe have been slightly forgotten. I think a war crimes Tribunal, and I'm specifically referring here to the permanent International Criminal Court that has been set up in The Hague, needs to bear in mind that a witness at a war crimes tribunal is not the same as a witness in a normal civil court. I'm aware that two, at least two victim witnesses were flown twice to The Hague and then flown back again without having been able to give their testimony. I believe that is doing those people a further injustice to the injustices that they've already faced during the wars that they are willing to testify on. Separately, this is the sixth time I have given evidence at this tribunal. It is the first time that I have been asked to speak to the lawyers of the defendant or in this case the defendant himself beforehand. I was willing to do so. It was noticeable to me or it has been during these days that none of the questions I was posed when I met Mr. Karadzic in prison were ever asked in the court and that he could have shown me the decency and the courtesy of showing me the documents that he was going to bring before me in the court, but he did not do so. This is strange to me, because Prosecution and Defence have the right to see documents, and I do not understand why a witness should not have that right as well. And lastly, when one of Your Honours suggested that the documents that Mr. Karadzic was going to be using in the days ahead should be given to me for, I believe, my night-time reading was the quote that I was given, I did read those documents and they were then not brought up in court at all, leaving me to wonder why I had been given them to read. That's all I would like to say to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations. Thank you again for your coming yet again to the Tribunal to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break now and -- for 25 minutes, and then we'll have another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. If you could take a solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please introduce yourself to the Court and tell us your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am Robert Donia. Last name is D-o-n-i-a. I am or have been intermittently over the past several years and expect to be again in the fall of this year a visiting professor of history at the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as a professor of history do you have any particular area of specialisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I have specialised in political and social history, principally of the 19th and 20th centuries, and principally in the area of south-eastern Europe, in particular Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard to your qualifications, could I ask that 65 ter 21894, page 121, be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that is an appendix to one of Dr. Donia's reports, which we'll be referring to more fully later. 21894, page 121.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you see Appendix A to your Sarajevo report on the screen on the monitor in front you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is that, CV, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as I look at page 1 on your CV, I note that you've written three books over the course of the last years: "Islam Under the Double Eagle," "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed," and "Sarajevo, a Biography." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I coauthored the second book, "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed," with John Fine, a professor of history at the University of Michigan also.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What are those books about, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The first book that you referenced, "Islam Under the Double Eagle," is a social and political history of the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Austro-Hungarian occupation from 1878 to 1914. The second book is a more general introductory history of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Middle Ages up until about -- up until 1994 when the book came out. And Sarajevo, a biography, is a history of the city of Sarajevo from its Ottoman origins to the very early twenty-first century.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to these books, perhaps I could ask you whether you could talk in a general way about the sources you exploited and relied on in your writings.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The sources that I've used in -- in these books and, for that matter, the various articles that I have done are very diverse. I use a lot of archival sources, and in particular for the first and third books that you've mentioned have worked in multiple archives both in the former Yugoslavia and neighbouring countries and other countries of Europe and -- and also in the US. I also use heavily the periodical press and the secondary literature by scholars both from the region and from outside the region which pertain to the topic that I'm addressing. And, of course, a lot of published document collections and various collections of articles and conference papers that deal with topics that I'm working with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any command of the Bosnian Serbian Croatian language, what we commonly refer to as B/C/S within the walls of this building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'd say I speak it well. I read it well. I write it with some difficulty, and probably have considerable difficulty reading handwritten Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you can read the language both in Cyrillic and Latin script then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Next I'd like to refer to some of your reports, three of which bring you here today. The first is entitled: "The Origins of the Republika Srpska, 1990 to 1992."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record and Your Honours, that's 65 ter number 11699.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second is entitled: "Thematic Excerpts from the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, 1991 to 1996," 65 ter number 11700. And the third, Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo, 1990, to 1995," the number of which I've already mentioned, 65 ter 21894. Now, Dr. Donia, could you explain briefly to the Trial Chamber what these three various reports are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. You've identified them in the chronological order in which they were prepared. The first report, "Origins of Republika Srpska," I prepared some years ago. I guess I've lost track of exactly the years, but nearly a decade ago, I believe, for the Krajisnik case, and prepared the second report for the Stanisic/Simatovic case originally. That report is a selection of excerpts from the transcripts of the Assembly of Republika Srpska or what I call the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And the third one, which is the history of the Sarajevo area and siege and war, I prepared for -- for this case about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to move on to your methodology, and you've alluded to that in your Sarajevo report at pages 4 to 6, I think. Perhaps you could tell us what is it that you as a historian do. What's your craft?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think fundamentally I prepare narratives, narratives which follow a particular progression, typically divided into thematic sections, and each thematic section attempts to elucidate a sequence of events, the causes of those events, and the linkages between them to produce a coherent story of events and the topic concerned. That's what essentially most professional historians do, although they may also do other things and address problems or issues that arise in the course of preparation of such narratives. The purpose of that narrative, then, is to acquaint a reader who is unfamiliar with the geography or chronology of the time and space concerned to gain some context and background about the area and the time about which the narrative is prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this narrative format that you've discussed the format you adopted for your origins of the Republika Srpska report and your Sarajevo report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and that -- those two reports rely on a very wide variety of source material and often call upon the words of the principal actors in their -- in their own expressions but are primarily designed to tell that story, to pull that narrative together.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is the second report, "Thematic Excerpts from the Assembly of the Republika Srpska," and I think I'll -- just so I don't have to say a mouthful every time I refer to the report I might call that one the excerpts report, is your excerpts report different in any regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is different in that it relies upon a single source, although the information within that source has been richly cross-checked with other sources for the period of times -- periods of time concerned, but although it relies on a single source, it is in it's own way a narrative, because I've broken it down into eight topical areas presented, then, in chronological order, what I judge to be the most revealing and helpful excerpts from the Assembly minutes, which is a voluminous collection of many thousands of pages, I'm not sure how many, but it's long, with the intent of creating exactly that kind of a narrative so that a reader could follow the progression of people's thinking and their own understanding of events at the time, a contemporaneous understanding as opposed to a retrospective one and one which captured then in their own words their own explanations and perceptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the subject of your sources, first of all, more generally speaking, and you alluded to this in your Sarajevo report but perhaps you could enlarge upon it, does anything guide or inform you in your selection of sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, and I codified basically what I think most or every historian uses as guideline for assessing sources, and number one is relevance. Is a particular document relevant to the question being examined in the narrative? Second, is its source, its origins, its provenance, the preparer or creator of the document. And third is its cross-checkability, if I can use the word, its verifiability in terms of other events related in other sources at the same time or in other sources retrospectively. And fourth is richness. I think that the -- an important and often unspoken criterion is does this document tell me something significant? Does it really enlighten and enrich mine and the reader's understanding of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions in your excerpts report -- now, how do the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions then fit within these four criteria?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, certainly their provenance is very clear. They were, as I understand it, delivered to the Tribunal by the secretary of the of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. Large parts of them are, frankly, not relevant, that is of the Assembly sessions themselves, and significant parts are relevant. So I've tried to focus on those parts that are relevant. In terms of cross-checking with contemporary sources, these transcripts are very well attested to by linking events with other contemporary sources. I'd give it high grades in that respect. And probably most illuminatingly they are extremely rich. They really provide -- they allow you to get into the mind of the people who were speaking at the time, understand what their philosophy was, what drove their decision-making, and what debates they had about various policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now I'll move on to another theme that comes up in -- particularly in two of your reports, your Sarajevo report and your excerpts report, and that's the subject of the strategic objectives, and I'd like to call up a document, please, and while we wait for that ask you a question if I may, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 17509, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, perhaps I could ask you to give us some background on these strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I now see the B/C/S version of the strategic -- and the English version of the strategic goals on the screen. The document that we're looking at is an excerpt from the Official Gazette of the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, published this particular -- this particular issue in November of 1993. The document reflects the approval of the strategic goals at an Assembly session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 12 May 1992. The Assembly at that time, after a lengthy exposition of the goals by various leaders of the Republika Srpska, approved the six goals that are -- that are before us. The fact that it was published in 1993 indicates that it still was -- reflected the time that -- or the assessment of the leaders that these were important goals that should be publicly known and that they had not changed. They basically had been in place since 1992. The -- in fact, the ideals that undergird the strategic goals were expressed in many speeches by various leaders in the Assembly and in other speeches well prior to 12 May 1992 and are referenced repeatedly and consistently as a foundation for decision-making within the Assembly from 1993, November 1993, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to -- if I may, perhaps I could ask that this first document, 17509, be admitted as the next exhibit. And while we wait for that, if I could ask for 65 ter number 00026, page 9, to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as can be P955, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now while we wait for 65 ter 00026, page 9, which, in fact, is an excerpt from the 12 May 1992 Assembly session, perhaps I could ask you, Dr. Donia, what was that Assembly session about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, can I just point out that the prior document that we looked at, the B/C/S was, in fact, a typed script of the original text of the proclamation which I have seen in its original and examined as a part of the Official Gazette. And your question was what was the 12th -- or the 16th Assembly session -- yes. And I recognise this as -- as a page from the actual original transcript of the 16th Assembly session on May 12th, 1992. That Assembly session was the first Assembly session to meet after the war had begun and after, in fact, much of the territorial gains had been secured by the various military and police and party forces of the Bosnian Serb nationalists. So it's a -- I think of it as a -- almost as a celebratory session in which delegates congratulate one another but also speak to what the key essential objectives of the Bosnian Serbs -- of the Serb people are in Bosnia, and therefore it's a kind of a founding Assembly for wartime, the pursuit of wartime goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware whether there were military leaders, Bosnian Serb military leaders, in attendance at this session?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic was certainly there. He gave a lengthy speech following Dr. Karadzic's talk to the Assembly, and there were a number of other people there in uniform we know from references, and I believe there were a few other general officers in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, the previous document was typed by whom? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated a few moments ago that you recognised the document on the screen in front of you, and for the record I'll say again this is an excerpt of the 12 May 1992 Assembly session, and I'd like to direct our attention to what I think is the first full paragraph on English page 9 which reads: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the Government, the Council for National Security, which we have set up, have formulated the strategic priorities," and further. And on the B/C/S page, I can't quite see the paragraph break to the left-hand side of the page, but my notation is that the same quote appears on page 8 of the B/C/S page, the first full paragraph on page 8. Now, Dr. Donia, this is an excerpt by -- speech by Dr. Karadzic, and you indicated you recognised it. Could you then tell us more precisely what it is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The -- the -- just looking at the B/C/S, this begins on the next to bottom line in what I'm looking at anyway, and I see now it's been scrolled up so it is there as a paragraph which appears to be the same as the exert that you just read. The statement in this paragraph is that Dr. Karadzic is indicating that the key elements of the -- the key institutions of the Bosnian Serb state have set forth these goals, have formulated them, on behalf of the Serbian people, and then states the first goal, which is, as he puts it, separation from the other two national communities, separation of states.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on to the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me. Your Honour. Pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on to the next paragraph which begins, "The second strategic goal," do you have any comment on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the second strategic goal is a key statement that the Bosnian Serbs want a contiguous territory based on a corridor of land between Semberija, which is to the -- in the very north-east of Bosnia, and Krajina which is in the north-west of Bosnia, and that corridor of land, as Dr. Karadzic expresses it here, not only links the two parts of eastern and Western Bosnia, which the Serbs held at that time, but also links the Serb-held territory in neighbouring Croatia to the west and the republic -- republics of Serbia and Montenegro to the east. Thus the corridor is a key linkage between what I think of these as two lung-like state territories to the east and west, but also a link between and among neighbouring polities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Neighbouring polities being who?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian -- I'm sorry. The neighbouring polities being the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was the Serb-held part of Croatia, and the republics of Serbia and Montenegro to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go on to the next paragraph which reads, "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina valley, that is, elimination of the Drina as a border between our two worlds." Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, this third strategic goal speaks to the eastern border area of Bosnia and proposes that the Drina, which -- much of which had served as a boundary between the Republic of Serbia or originally the principality of Serbia and the Kingdom of Serbia and Bosnia, it served that capacity since the 1830s, be eliminated as a boundary which would mean that there would be then no boundary between the Serb-held area of eastern Bosnia and the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to just one more of the strategic objectives, and it requires us to move over to the next English page and the next B/C/S page; that being the fifth strategic goal, division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts. Could you go over to the next English page, please. Now, Dr. Donia, do you see the top line that reads: "Sarajevo is strategically in the fifth place, but the battle in Sarajevo and for Sarajevo, seen strategically and tactically, is of decisive importance because it does not allow the establishment of even the illusion of a state. Alija does not have a state while we have part of Sarajevo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on this passage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The strategic goal of separation as it pertained to Sarajevo, the capital city and largest city in Bosnia, in fact, had in Dr. Karadzic's articulation some specific features; namely, in recognition of its status as the capital, he valued this separation of the city as a way of crippling or denying -- crippling the state or denying to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the attributes of a state, and Sarajevo in that sense sort of crystallises into a specific area the general goal that was expressed as the first strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are my questions with respect to this excerpt from the 16th Assembly session, and I would at this point like to ask Your Honours for admission of those pages, but I understand - and I haven't been present in court for these rulings - but I understand Your Honours' guidance as being for documents contemporaneous as this one obviously is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This minute it will be admitted in its entirety and which in particular will be used in the later stage. For the convenience, it's much better to admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're now tendering this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty-six -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, I note the original copy of that Official Gazette which contains the strategic objectives was admitted as Exhibit P781, but the current one we received is a typed version. So because the format is different we'll admit them both. And we'll admit this transcription or minute of this session as --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P956, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies with respect to that last document. I think it was a situation where we had different versions of the same document and I wasn't aware. My apologies to the Court and Mr. Registrar. But I must say, I've received the same information at the same moment Your Honours did. So my thanks to my colleagues who are watching remotely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, if I may, we've gone through each of these objectives in a little bit of detail now, and I want to go back to the first one and ask you, sir, how would you characterise this first objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is expressed as a general principle, but it has many possible, let's say specific, components to it. It clearly embraces the separation of the national communities but does not specify whether that separation is to be territorial, physical, organisational, or institutional, or human, or some combination of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you seen articulations in the course of your research as to the nature of separation that was contemplated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I endeavoured to put some of those in those that were -- a selection of those that were referenced in transcript of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in the excerpts report, as we've called it, the excerpts from the Assembly of Republika Srpska. They also occur in a number of speeches and declarations reported in the periodical press, and in both cases they occur before and after the principles actually adopted as the first strategic goal on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then if you've seen some evidence, what type of separation was contemplated, territorial, physical, organisational, institutional, or human?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I meant to say institutional as covering organisational, but I find indications that what was intended was all four, and in some articulations there are two or three that are included or only one, but in a few cases all four are indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Articulations by the accused?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: By the accused and other leaders of the Bosnian Serb -- of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who in particular? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, we find the principle endorsed by General Mladic. We find it embraced by Dr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik, among others.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could perhaps then have P956 brought up on the screen again. I'd like to take us to pages 4546 of the English translation and 3839 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, Dr. Donia, on the screen before us is a passage containing comments by Mr. Krajisnik, who you've just referred to. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page in English, please. The -- pardon me for one moment -- seventh line up from the bottom we see Mr. Krajisnik's statement to the effect that: "The first goal is the most important one, and in relation to all other goals, all other goals are sub-items of the first one." Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think that's a self-evident comment on his part as the first strategic goal really is a general principle and governs in principle the other goals that were expressed in -- in two through six. The notion that the first strategic goal was, let's say, the founding one, the essential principle, I think is reflected in the number of times that it gets cited and recited in other Assembly sessions following this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, referring to other Assembly sessions, perhaps I could turn now to your excerpts report and ask to display a passage from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 11700, pages -- e-court pages 30 to 31, I think, paragraph 73. And this should be an extract -- if we could move further. It's paragraph 73, please. You're at paragraph 65 now. And move forward in English I would guess two pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There. At the bottom of the page we see, Dr. Donia, as cited in your report, an extract from the 56th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, dated 17 December 1995, which is a quote by Mr. Krajisnik. Could you read that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first say that I think I have been defeated by the system in that I tried to make the footnote numbers correspond to the paragraph numbers so that the B/C/S would be readily apparent in the original report and clearly I have failed in that endeavour, but to read this particularly -- particular excerpt from the Assembly session held right at the time that the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed in Paris: "The task of this republic and the first strategic goal is that we separate from Muslims and Croats and no one has the right to base the strategy of Srpsko Sarajevo --"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: " -- on remaining in a joint country. Therefore, any danger or wish for connection and solution of Sarajevo in which we will stay with Muslims and Croats is out of the question. No one can make a new decision now, according to which we will stay together. Neither do the people in Sarajevo want that, that is to say, the people or the leadership of Sarajevo, but the flaw of our members of parliament is that they see -- is that they see the danger if we stay in the Muslim-Croat Federation, and Sarajevo would be the connection point keeping the union together." Let me just say that this was a statement in response to a speech of another delegate or sequential to it in which a delegate had proposed that in the -- in accord with the post-Dayton change of -- of borders, of boundaries, that the -- instead of moving all the Serbs out of Sarajevo that the Republika Srpska relocate some of its governing institutions into the federation where Serbs were then living. So he was proposing, was this other delegate, a policy that deviated from the strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note that Mr. Krajisnik made this statement some three years into the war after he made a similar statement you just referred to on May 12th, 1992. Do you have any comment in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he actually made this statement when the war was over and still insisted that the strategic goal was valid and, in fact, could not be violated in the post-war relocations that he foresaw.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could move to another area now, still related to the strategic objectives. And in talking about, in particular, the second objective, you referred the Judges to different areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wonder if it would assist if we called up a map, P727. And while we wait for that map, perhaps I could ask you to enlarge on the question of the strategic objectives in the following way: Are they territorially defined?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The second through the sixth goals do, in fact, define territories, although the exact territory being defined is not very specific. The second goal, of course, defining a corridor, the two other goals speaking about borders on rivers or no borders on rivers, and the outlet to the sea very vague, but there was some agreement on -- on where that corridor to the sea would ideally go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you think, Dr. Donia, if my colleagues from the registry were able to enlarge Bosnia and Herzegovina on this map in front of you, you might be able to roughly illustrate for Their Honours - oh, well done. Thank you very much - the territory generally encompassed by the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I could certainly identify the boundaries that were specified. Defining the exact territory is a little more difficult, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I invite you to do that with the pen from the side of the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is fancy. This is good. Let me start with the Drina River. The Drina River begins inside Bosnia. I believe it's about -- excuse me. It's about here somewhere and then becomes the border, the eastern border of Bosnia. I'm sorry, I went too far. And therefore -- and for the, let's say all but its first couple dozen kilometres defines the boundary between Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Dr. Donia for the record has made a marking in red line on the far right side of the map of Bosnia. And -- well, I was just about to ask Dr. Donia, as indicated, that he went a little bit too far, and as I recall e-court, we may be able to remove that last line, too far, that he tried to correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. It goes up about to here. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've delineated, I take it from what you've said, one boundary?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that was the boundary that was to be abolished in the goal that referred to the Drina River. The other rivers that were to serve as boundaries were the Neretva, which starts here but actually kind of gains some significance as it goes to Mostar and down to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia's made an upside down U shape in the middle of the map from the centre of the territory to the sea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And to the Sava River, which comes down from Croatia and proceeds along the very -- constitutes the northern boundary of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Referring at this last passage to the line across the top of the territory of the former republic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there a boundary that lay to the west at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, and you're going to have to give me the name of the river here to evoke my geography skills.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Una --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- was one of the rivers mentioned in these objectives.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, and the Una --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Number four.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- runs along the western part of the republic and goes inland to run through Bihac and up to the -- to merge with the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could I invite you, Dr. Donia, to put your initials on one corner of the map with today's date, which is 31 May.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this territory that you've depicted as encompassing the -- encompass by the strategic objectives, was that territory meant to be contiguous?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the second strategic goal really spelled out that this territory, whatever else it would be, would, in fact, be contiguous, that it would link, as I described it, the two saddle bags to the east and west. That corridor then running sort of to the -- along the northern part of Bosnia and, in particular, the area of Brcko was its narrowest point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Dr. Donia has made a double line now to the top right. That would be the north-east corner of this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, territorially speaking, do -- if we look at this map do these goals represent potential links to areas outside the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was the question again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Territorially speaking, then, do these goals represent potential links to outside the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, and the second goal and the Drina goal, which I think was the fourth, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could tender this map as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P957.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the fifth objective and the city of Sarajevo, I'd like to ask for another map which has been entered previously. It has the number 815, P815.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we wait for P815, perhaps I could ask you, Dr. Donia, to -- ah, and there's P815 in front of us. Perhaps with the assistance of P815 I wonder if I could invite you to provide a brief explanation of the development of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. I don't need another drawing disaster here. The city of Sarajevo developed from -- in this -- this east-west valley starting at the extreme eastern end, and I'll just put a circle, perhaps -- that was gorgeous. Where the -- following along the river there to the area in orange, one sees a little crook in the river, and that really is the place where as an urban settlement in the Ottoman period, in the 1400s, Sarajevo first was founded, and from there the city grew to the west or the left of the map that we're looking at and reached about a kilometre and a half by the end of the Ottoman period, which was 1878, and filled in substantially then with the Austro-Hungarian period until 1918. And then really the major development of the city to the west from that point on took place in the Socialist period or the Communist period after 1945. That development was actually very rapid and consistent over the period from 1945 to 1990 and included some expansion into the hills on either side of the city, that is to the north and to the south, and to the peripheral areas of the city, some of which are shown here, some are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you, Doctor. Just before you go further, before the drawing disaster as you had described it, I should have asked you and omitted: Do you recognise what's depicted on the screen in front of you here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is a map essentially of the most developed area of Sarajevo with an indication on it of the boundaries of the municipalities that made up the city, or some of them, some of those municipalities as of 1990, in fact, the period from 1977 to 1990, and also an approximation of the lines of the siege from about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the rapid development that you've just described have any effect on the municipalities in the area of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The relationship between municipalities, which is the fundamental administrative unit used in the Socialist period, and cities is very diverse in Yugoslavia in the Socialist period. Sarajevo in the early years of socialism consisted of four municipalities. Those were Stari Grad or Old Town to the extreme right of our map, Novo Sarajevo, and then to the lower left of the map Ilidza, and at the very top of the map Vogosca. Ilidza and Vogosca were essentially standalone municipalities linked to the city, but they were economically largely self-sufficient, Ilidza being a kind of resort area, Vogosca being more industrial. In 1977, the city -- the map of the city changed with -- in accord with the urban plan that was developed in -- in 1976. The two inner municipalities of Stari Grad and Novo Sarajevo had become very densely populated, and in order to bring government closer to the population and also to rationalise the growth of communications and transport facilities and industrialisation, the -- the city fathers divided Stari Grad into two municipalities, one which retained the name Stari Grad or Old City, and the second one called Centar. They then further divided Novo Sarajevo into keeping the same name, Novo Sarajevo, and a new area known as Novi Grad, or New City, to the upper left part of the map. In addition, the city acquired four existing municipalities which were largely rural in character. Those were Hadzici, Pale, Ilijas, and -- help me with number four here. Trnovo. Trnovo. So that rounded out the ten municipalities that made up the city of Sarajevo in the period from 1977 to 1990. Now, there was then a -- kind of an umbrella city of Sarajevo government which had its own Assembly and brought together the delegates from these ten different municipalities. So in a sense the city had a two-tiered organisation, the municipalities that made up the city and the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This concept --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about municipalities as regards Sarajevo. This term "municipality," what did it mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The municipality, or "opstina" in B/C/S, is -- was the name for -- given in the latter part of socialism to a fundamental unit, administrative unit, that dates back to late Ottoman times, and that administrative unit was a -- typically a small town or even a larger town which was -- which bore the same name as the municipality and was surrounded by agricultural land, undeveloped land, socially owned land, and typically peasant villages. The structure of the municipality, of course in the case of Sarajevo, took on a somewhat different character, but still the idea was that there was a seat of government located in some area that was the -- the centre or near the centre of the municipality, and the municipality was conceived of as and built to be a unit that was rationally geographic, economic, and administrative so that its rationale were essentially those three criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was ethnicity a factor in this concept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it was not. The purpose of the plan, for example, of 1976 was to try to develop the economy on a more rational basis so that many of the productive facilities, factories, were moved outside of the city, the central city, to peripheral municipalities with the thought of bringing -- with the intent of bringing the means of production closer to the workers. There was no ethnic component or any discussion of ethnicity about that design at the time. It was, in fact, an effort by the city fathers to make the city more attractive as a competitor for the 1984 Winter Olympics. So ethnicity in the overall picture of municipality boundaries played no role or very little role in the actual design of where boundaries were placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this answer you've, I think, alluded to Sarajevo when you refer to the Winter Olympics, and when you say ethnicity in the overall picture of municipal boundaries played no role or little role in the actual design of where boundaries were placed, is that also in reference to Sarajevo or is that throughout the former republic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I'd say it's throughout the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ethnicity really was not a consideration. Sometimes people would talk about cultural factors as a -- as a role in the design of the municipality map with the intent of having cultural facilities convenient to large blocks of population. So that's what I meant by -- that might have been an indirect consideration of ethnicity, but generally speaking, it was an economic, geographic, and administrative concept throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic or other SDS leaders express opinions about this concept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think from the late 1980s, perhaps even earlier, the Serb nationalist thinkers, in Sarajevo in particular, developed a critique of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Communist era that included the critique of the municipal structure, and their contention was, and I would point to a number of early speeches by Dr. Karadzic in which he expressed this view, their contention was that the municipalities had been drawn to the disadvantage of the Serb people. Croats in Bosnia, some of them also voiced the view that municipalities were developed to the disadvantage of the Croatian people. The critique surfaced into, I think, public discourse in the early days of the election campaign starting in about the summer -- or starting in the summer of 1990 and thereafter became, I think, an important part of the Serb nationalist programme for the SDS and particularly the SDS leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps at this point we could turn to another map, and that will be final map for today, P783, on the subject of municipality structures. Do you see the map on the screen in front of you, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I used it, referred to it a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you then tell us what it is, please, and what it represents.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This map shows the 109 municipalities that made up Bosnia and Herzegovina in the year 1991 at the time of the census. I liked the map because it's extremely difficult, in fact impossible, to capture the ethnic distribution of people's in Bosnia on a two-dimensional object in any map, but this one to me -- to my mind comes perhaps closer than -- than most to capturing that, because it shows you not only -- it shows you for each municipality not only the group that has an absolute or a relative majority in that municipality, but also gives you on the bar charts the other groups, including those that are --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, could I just stop you for a moment. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we've just lost the picture of the map that was on the screen. Please continue. I'm sorry about the interruption, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The bar graphs, the vertical bars, show the secondary, tertiary and sometimes fourth group, given that there were a significant number of people who in the 1981 and 1991 census declared themselves as others or Yugoslavs. So one gets a sense from this map not only of what the largest group was in a municipality, that is held an absolute or relative majority, but also what the composition of others -- other groups was in that municipality. Unfortunately, it doesn't go below the municipal level to show that, but it does at the municipal level show what the population distribution was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you relate the population distribution as depicted on this map to the boundaries of the strategic objectives that you depicted earlier for us? Does the territory encompassed by the strategic objectives cover multi-ethnic areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, insofar as we can determine from the strategic objectives what was intended in territorial terms. For example, the east-west corridor, which was an inherent part of -- which was the essence of strategic goal number two, runs across the very north part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as one could see from this map, those numerous municipalities sort of in the upper right-hand part of the map, right where that corridor would have to run, were indeed very mixed in composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, what about the city of Sarajevo, Dr. Donia? I recall in your Sarajevo report you said that it embodied the human diversity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. What I just said about a map not capturing the diversity of identity and the complexity of identity for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina goes doubly so for Sarajevo, and there is an effort here just on -- to the lower right of the -- of the map, a separate representation of Sarajevo, which frankly is not very good because it's not complete, but even just a glance at that shows that there are few areas in the city of Sarajevo that are ethnically homogenous, and, in fact, the complexity ranges -- it gets particularly pronounced in the areas of the city that were settled and built up after 1945, because those housing settlements were largely high-rise apartment buildings, and so people were living on various floors of apartment buildings without any ethnic differentiation whatever. Now, that is true of part of the city. Other parts of the city as it was created with the ten municipalities in 1977 were more rural but were nevertheless very complex in their ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll adjourn for today, and we will continue tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
